For instance, perceptions of attractiveness mostly converge cross-culturally, despite cultural differences in beauty standards (e.g. Kara & Özgür, 2023).

Still, there is considerable cross-cultural variation in the strength and exact manifestation of halo effects for different attributes due to differences in locally perceived violence (Borras-Guevara et al., 2017), pathogen prevalence, and mate preferences (DeBruine et al., 2010; Gangestad et al., 2006; Penton-Voak et al., 2004; Thornhill & Fincher, 2014). For example, the trade-off theory (DeBruine et al., 2010) suggests that women's preference for masculine men depends on the assessment of potential costs (e.g. low paternal investment) and benefits (e.g. healthier offspring via genetic benefits). One prediction of this theory is that a poorer public healthcare system or higher pathogen prevalence lead to stronger masculinity preferences (see also DeBruine et al., 2012). Hence, especially for men, perceived attractiveness should be more strongly associated with perceived physical dominance (as a proxy of masculinity) in cultures with higher pathogen prevalence or a poorer healthcare system (DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004; but see Jones et al., 2021 and Lee et al., 2025 for conflicting evidence). For both sexes, such high-risk environments increase the value of mating partners with good genetic fitness and health, to which physical attractiveness has been proposed to be a cue. Therefore, the association between perceived attractiveness and perceived health for both men and women should be stronger within cultures with higher pathogen prevalence and poorer public healthcare systems.

Halo effects may vary cross-culturally along the collectivism-individualism dimension (Hofstede, 1980; Minkov et al., 2017). Collectivism is characterised by individuals being integrated into groups from an early age and strongly defining themselves through their relationship with others, emphasising group cohesion and loyalty (Triandis, 1999). On the other hand, individualism is characterised by looser relationships with others and by the selfdefinition being more strongly related to autonomy, self-reliance, and differentiation from others (Triandis, 1999; Triandis et al., 1990). Social perception (Bond & Forgas, 1984; Forgas & Bond 1985) as well as self-perception (Bond & Cheung, 1983; Cousins, 1989; Triandis et al., 1990) vary between individuals from collectivistic versus individualistic cultures. In a study of US white, US black, and Korean students, Zebrowitz et al. (1993) found strong agreements in ratings of attractiveness. However, for ratings of honesty, dominance, and warmth, associations were more diverse. In combination with their findings of attractiveness halo effects differing by the associated attributes (e.g. submissiveness, warmth, honesty), the authors concluded that a general halo effect may be universal but the highly esteemed traits are not.

Thus, the halo effect might manifest differently across cultural contexts, as different traits might be perceived as important or desirable.

Similarly, Wheeler and Kim (1997) argued that the halo effect varies across cultures, and that physical attractiveness should be more strongly associated with traits valued in that culture. Building on the study by Zebrowitz et al. (1993), Wheeler and Kim (1997) compared ratings of collectivistic (Korean) to those of individualistic (US American and Canadian) students. They found that in the individualistic cultures, attractiveness was related to potency, whilst in the collectivistic culture it was related to traits of integrity and concern for others.

Similarly, in Shaffer et al.'s (2000) study, US American students rated attractive targets' individualistic traits (e.g. optimism, selfishness) as higher, whilst Taiwanese students rated them higher on collectivistic traits (e.g. cooperativeness, friendliness). However, most of these studies did not adopt a fully cross-cultural perspective, as they examined cultural differences in either observers or targets, but not in both. Even the recent extensive study by Batres and Shiramizu (2023) comprised only one mixed-ethnicity sample of targets (consisting of Asian, Black, Latin, and White faces) which were all judged by observers from 45 countries.

Observers judge the faces of different ethnicities more superficially or with less motivation due to the own-race effect, possibly because of greater within-ethnicity exposure (Tanaka et al., 2004). Also, genetic relatedness, indicated by facial similarity, crucially influences social judgments (Todorov et al., 2015). These aspects may lead to stronger agreement in intra-than for intercultural judgments, which is explicable by greater intracultural familiarity and culture-specific perceptual learning (Zebrowitz et al., 2012). Hence, the ownrace effect suggests that studies investigating observers or targets from a single ethnicity can provide only limited information on cross-cultural stability and differences in halo effects.

Our preregistered study provides a broader view on cross-cultural convergence and divergence in facial judgments of socially relevant attributes. It includes both observers and targets from two populations, Brazil and Germany, that differ on several cultural dimensions, including collectivism-individualism and human development (World Population Review, 2026). Brazil's population is more collectivistic, with a score of -56 on the individualismcollectivism dimension (factor score multiplied by 100) and a rank of 40 out of 56 countries, according to Minkov et al. (2017), and is characterised by high interdependence and a strong emphasis on familial and communal ties (Carlo et al., 2007). Germany's population is more individualistic, with a score of 102 and a rank of 7 (Minkov et al., 2017), and is characterized by a stronger focus on autonomy, lower levels of interdependence (Özkarar-Gradwohl et al., 2020), and a higher degree of human development and well-being compared with Brazil (World Population Review, 2026). These earlier findings motivated the present comparison. At the same time, a two-country design cannot isolate individualism-collectivism from other socioecological differences between the populations.

Study Aim and Hypotheses

We aimed to replicate and extend earlier findings on the attractiveness halo effect based on faces (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Eagly et al., 1991; Feingold, 1992; Langlois et al., 2000), focusing on cross-population and target sex differences. As suggested by Kordsmeyer et al. (2024), our study fills a research gap by providing a more focussed cross-population perspective drawing on both observers and targets from a non-Western, more collectivistic (Brazil) and a Western, more individualistic country (Germany, Minkov et al., 2017; Pelham et al., 2022). We offer a comprehensive approach by examining a relatively large number of socially relevant attributes, including two facets of dominance, social and physical, reflecting the multifaceted nature of dominance (e.g. Bryan et al., 2011), in contrast to earlier studies which treated dominance as a unitary construct (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008).

Based on previous findings, we investigated the following preregistered hypotheses: 1. Perceived facial attractiveness is positively associated with perceived social dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity.

2. A positive association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance is hypothesised in male targets judged by Brazilian observers (based on the trade-off theory; null correlation in male targets judged by German observers).

For female targets, we hypothesise a negative association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance.

3. Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived health are stronger for Brazilian compared to German observers (based on a purportedly higher pathogen prevalence and poorer public healthcare system in Brazil compared to Germany, Celestino et al., 2021; Salmanton-García et al., 2025; Warnecke et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2025a , 2025b). 4. For male targets specifically, associations between perceived facial attractiveness and perceived prosociality are stronger for Brazilian than for German observers; for female targets, associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived prosociality do not differ across observers' nationalities (Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997).

5. Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived intelligence and perceived familiarity are stronger for female compared to male targets (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Kniffin et al., 2014). 6. Interobserver agreements for all attributes are stronger intra-than inter-culturally (i.e. stronger for Brazilian observers judging Brazilian faces and German observers judging German faces compared to German observers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian observers judging German faces, based on the own-race effect). 7. There are positive correlations between ratings by Brazilian and German observers for all attributes for the same faces, except for perceived familiarity, for which we hypothesised a null correlation.

Method

Targets' Facial Photographs

As part of earlier studies involving further variables not relevant to this study ([blinded for peer review]), facial photographs were available from 116 Brazilian target men (age: M = 24.2 years, SD = 7.5, range 18-63, age data were unavailable for 8 men), and 149 Brazilian target women (age: M = 26.6 years, SD = 9.9, range 18-65, age data were unavailable for 9 women), 164 German target men (age: M= 24.2 years, SD = 3.2, range 18-34), and 154 German target women (age: M = 22.4 years, SD = 4.2, range 18-53). Two facial photographs were taken of Brazilian targets while standing in front of a white or grey wall at a distance of two meters, with the participants directly facing the camera (Canon EOS T6i) with the focus set to 50mm.

They were instructed to maintain a neutral expression and wear standardised clothing. For each German target, two facial photographs were taken while standing in front of a white wall at a distance of two meters, with the participants directly facing the camera (Canon EOS 350D) and showing a neutral facial expression. For all targets, the more suitable of the two photos, in terms of a neutral facial expression and standardized head position, was chosen.

For Brazilian observers only, to reduce observer strain and because compensation was not possible due to legal restrictions in Brazil, the final samples of 164 German target men, 154 German target women, and 149 Brazilian female (but not the sample of 116 Brazilian male targets) were randomly divided into two sets of 82 German target men, 77 German target women, and 74-75 Brazilian target women each. Separate groups of Brazilian observers rated these two sets, whereas German observers rated the full sets of facial photos, as outlined below.

All photos of Brazilian and German targets were delineated horizontally based on pupils (standardising for inter-pupillary distance) using WebMorph (DeBruine, 2018). Previews of all photographs (separately for each of the four subsamples of Brazilian and German male and female targets, with each photo being displayed for 0.4 seconds one after another) were created using MiniTool MovieMaker Free (MiniTool, 2024).

Simulation-based sensitivity power analyses (1000 simulations) conducted using the package simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016) in a cross-classified multilevel model (including random intercepts for targets and observers) suggested that the smallest (116) and largest (164) target sample size would allow to detect small effect sizes of β ≥ 0.12 and β ≥ 0.10, respectively, with 80 % power at α = 0.05 (one-tailed for preregistered hypotheses, Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016). For interaction effects in hypotheses 3-5, the power analyses yielded effect sizes of β≥0.14 to be detected with 80 % power for the smallest sample size for the interaction between observer nationality and perceived attractiveness (N = 116 Brazilian male targets, hypotheses 3-4), and of β≥0.10 for the smallest sample size for the interaction between target sex and perceived attractiveness (N = 265 Brazilian male and female targets, hypothesis 5).

Observers

A total of 893 observers from Brazil and Germany evaluated the target faces. The Brazilian sample comprised 270 men (age: M = 36.1 years, SD = 15.5, range = 18-89) and 301 women (age: M = 38.0 years, SD = 13.7, range = 18-76). The German sample comprised 162 men (age: M = 30.6 years, SD = 11.6, range = 19-73) and 160 women (age: M = 30.9 years, SD = 13.1, range = 19-72). Different groups of 9-12 observers rated the faces separately for each attribute, target sex, and target nationality. Following our preregistered procedure, we excluded overall seven individual observers (6 Brazilian men, 1 German man) whose removal increased the intraclass correlation of their group (i.e. for a given attribute and target-photo set) above the upper bound of the confidence interval. Table 1 reports the exact number of observers per attribute, target sex, and target nationality.

Rating Procedure

Brazilian participants were recruited via the [blinded for peer-review] newsletter and online social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram), and at the [blinded for peer-review]. They participated voluntarily without monetary compensation due to legal restrictions in Brazil.

German observers were primarily recruited at the [blinded for peer-review] via an email newsletter for individuals interested in psychological studies and through student groups on social media platforms. They were remunerated for their participation by monetary compensation or course credit.

Observers were only admitted to the study if they self-reported to be heterosexual (scoring 0-2 on a 7-point Kinsey scale with endpoints0 = "completely heterosexual" and6 = "completely homosexual", Kinsey et al., 1948) and cisgender (biological sex assigned at birth (female, male, or diverse) matching their gender identity (with the following response options: man, woman, nonbinary, transsexual man, transsexual woman, other); hence only participants indicating female or male as their biological sex and woman or man as their gender identity, respectively, were admitted to the study. Participants also reported their relationship status (single, open relationship, committed relationship, other), their employment status (student, intern/trainee, employed, unemployed, retired), their social class (low, mid-low, medium, midhigh, high), and the degree to which they were seeking a short-term partner currently (1-item Short-Term Seeking scale, "To what degree are you currently seeking a short-term mate (i.e. a one-night stand, a brief affair)?", 7-point scale with endpoints1 = "not at all currently seeking" and7 = "strongly currently seeking", Buss & Schmitt, 2007; Schmitt, 2003) as control variables.

Further, Brazilian participants were asked about their ethnic background (Black, mixed race ("pardo"), White, Indigenous, Arabic, Oriental) and in which city or state they grew up.

This was due to large demographic heterogeneity in Brazil (Hofstede et al., 2010), which affects how familiar they are with white, more northern European looking people (southern Brazilian states such as Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, and Paraná) or more mixed-ethnicity and black people (northern Brazilian states such as Bahia and Para) (Lins et al., 2010), and could therefore impact their perceptions of attractiveness, familiarity, and other attributes, which may in turn influence halo effects.

Instruments

The rating studies were conducted online using the survey software formr.org (Arslan et al., 2020). Targets' facial photographs were presented on computer screens. After selfreporting their biological sex and gender identity, observers were randomly allocated to one of the target group and attribute conditions (depending on their sex and gender; in case their sex and gender did not match, participants were excluded from further participation, to allow an unequivocal allocation to one study condition). Subsequently, they were asked to complete items on their demographics and to watch a preview of the whole subsample of photographs for a first impression of the range of all relevant faces. Afterwards, observers viewed the photos in randomised order, one at a time, for as long as they wanted, with the rating item and response scale being shown directly underneath each photo.

Attributes

All targets were judged on the following eight attributes using eleven-point Likert scales: (1) facial attractiveness by other-sex observers (i.e. female targets judged by male observers and vice versa, item: "How attractive is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all attractive", +5 = "very attractive"), (2) facial physical dominance by same-sex observers (item "How likely is it that this man/woman will win a fight against another man/woman?", adapted from Puts et al., 2006; Torrance et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2010, scale endpoints -5 = "very unlikely", +5 = "very likely"), (3) facial social dominance by same-sex observers (item "How likely is this man/woman to tell other people what to do, to be respected, influential, and to be a leader?", adapted from Puts et al., 2006; Torrance et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2010, scale endpoints -5 = "very unlikely", +5 = "very likely"), (4) facial prosociality by same-sex observers (aggregate of three items: "How trustworthy/compassionate/kind is this man/woman?", adapted from Kogan et al., 2014, scale endpoints -5 = "not at all trustworthy/compassionate/kind", +5 = "very trustworthy/compassionate/kind"), ( 5) facial health by same-sex observers (item "How healthy is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "very unhealthy", +5 = "very healthy"), ( 6) facial intelligence by other-sex observers (item "How intelligent is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all intelligent", +5 = "very intelligent"), ( 7) facial social competence by same-sex observers (item "How socially competent is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "very socially incompetent", +5 = "very socially competent"), ( 8) facial familiarity by same-sex observers (item "How familiar does this man/woman look to you?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all familiar", +5 = "very familiar").

Attractiveness and intelligence were judged by other-sex observers and the other attributes by same-sex observers, because they are prominent attributes in mate choice/intersexual selection and intrasexual competition, respectively (e.g. Puts, 2016).

Statistical Analysis

All analyses were performed using R (R Core Team, 2025) and the following packages: car (Fox & Weisberg, 2019), dplyr (Wickham et al., 2023), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), parameters (Lüdecke et al., 2020), psych (Revelle, 2024), and simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016).

To increase power and based on the partly low internal consistencies (see Table 2), we ran cross-classified multilevel models (e.g. Nestler & Back, 2017) with individual ratings for physical dominance, social dominance, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity nested in targets and observers, including a random intercept for target and observer (due to diverging numbers of observers between attractiveness and the other attributes, we used aggregate attractiveness ratings for each target) for hypotheses 1-5 (descriptions and results of preregistered analyses for hypotheses 1-5 based on aggregate ratings can be found in the supplement). As preregistered, preliminary analyses used t-tests to assess mean differences in ratings between Brazilian and German observers for each attribute and target group. For hypotheses 1-2, cross-classified multilevel models with perceived attractiveness as a fixed effect, random intercepts for target and observer, and a second attribute (perceived physical dominance, social dominance, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, or familiarity) as the outcome variablefoot_0 . Moderator effects of observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) (with perceived attractiveness and either observer nationality or target sex as the predictor variables plus their interaction term, and a second attribute as the outcome variable) were examined in cross-classified multilevel models, also including random intercepts for target and observer. As a direct proxy for one-tailed hypothesis tests at α = .05 (Lakens et al., 2018), 90% confidence intervals were calculated for ICCs to test differences in interobserver reliabilities (hypothesis 6). As preregistered, one-sided tests were used for directional hypotheses (Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016). To investigate the robustness of our findings, we ran partial correlations and multilevel models including the preregistered control variables target age (e.g. see Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014), target relationship status (binary: single vs. open relationship/committed relationship/engaged/married), and target BMI. As further control variables, we added targets' smiling (on a 3-point Likert scale with0 = "not smiling at all",1 = "slight smile", and2 = "bright smile", since smiling has been shown to influence perceptions of competence, for instance, Filkukova & Jorgensen, 2020), target men's beardedness (on a 11-point Likert scale from0 = "clean shaven" to10 = "longest, fullest beard", since beardedness is related to judgments of dominance, trustworthiness, and attractiveness, Dixson et al., 2024; Garza et al., 2024; plus there tends to be a difference in the degree of average beardedness between Brazil and European countries, Valentova, Varella, Bartova et al., 2017), as well as target women's make-up and jewellery (on a 11-point Likert scale from0 = "no make-up or jewellery" to10 = "prominent make-up and a lot of jewellery", which may especially influence perceptions of attractiveness, Mulhern et al., 2003; Schneider & Moron, 2023). Smiling, beardedness, make-up and jewellery were coded by three independent and trained assistants blind to the research question and hypotheses (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) ranges by target sample, for smiling: ICCs = .43-.86; beardedness: ICCs = .91-.97; make-up and jewellery: ICCs = .84-.93). (Koo & Li, 2016; Trebicky et al., 2023); Pros. = prosociality.

Results

Descriptive statistics for all Brazilian and German ratings and bivariate correlations of ratings between Brazilian and German observers as well as t-tests and Cohen's d effect sizes of average differences between Brazilian and German observers are shown in Table 3. Overall, ratings of Brazilian and German observers were weakly to strongly correlated (r = .25-.85) for all target groups except for familiarity ratings of male German targets (r = .04). Average ratings of Brazilian and German observers differed significantly for some target groups and attributes, with negligible to very large effects (see Table 3). Bivariate Pearson correlations of attractiveness with all other attributes are shown in Table S1, stratified by target group and observer nationality. For all target groups and both observer nationalities, perceived attractiveness was positively associated with perceived prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity (confirming hypothesis 1). Perceived attractiveness was positively associated with perceived intelligence for all target groups except for male Brazilian targets rated by Brazilian observers (for which we found a non-significant, yet positive association) and with perceived social dominance for all target groups except for female Brazilian targets judged by German observers (mostly in line with hypothesis 1). Finally, for perceived physical dominance, there were significant positive associations with perceived attractiveness for male targets across populations (i.e. for Germans judging Brazilians and for Brazilians judging Germans, not significant within-nationally, for German but not Brazilian targets in line with hypothesis 2), and significant negative associations for female targets (for both target nationalities, though only for male German observers, not significant for Brazilian observers, see Table 4, partially confirming hypothesis 2). Almost all associations remained virtually unchanged when controlling for age, smiling, make-up, glasses, beardedness, and the headband worn by Brazilian targets (except for the positive effect of attractiveness on social dominance for Brazilian females judged by Germans turning significant when including the control variables). Note. One-tailed p-values for effects based on preregistered directional hypotheses for all attributes except for male physical dominance judged by German observers; σ 2 , τ00target, τ00rater, and ICC denote random effects.

To test hypotheses 3 to 5 on cross-population and sex differences, interaction terms between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) were added to the multilevel models. For all four target group, the association between perceived attractiveness and health was significantly stronger for German compared to Brazilian observers (contrary to hypothesis 3, interaction term for male Brazilian targets: β = .17, SE = .04, t = 4.60, p < .001, σ2 = 3.89, τ00target = 0.18, τ00rater = 0.63, ICC = .17; male German targets: β = .09, SE = .03, t = 2.83, p = .005, σ2 = 5.05, τ00target = 0.62, τ00rater = 0.28, ICC = .15; female Brazilian targets: β = .17, SE = .03, t = 5.62, p < .001, σ2 = 4.26, τ00target = 0.83, τ00rater = 0.50, ICC = .24; female German targets: β = .10, SE = .04, t = 2.96, p = .003, σ2 = 5.03, τ00target = 0.48, τ00rater = 0.85, ICC = .21). For all target groups except for male Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction term between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality on prosociality, with a significantly stronger (positive) association for German observers, all contrary to hypothesis 4 (interaction term for female Brazilian targets: β = .13, SE = .03, t = 3.91, p < .001, σ2 = 3.46, τ00target = 0.68, τ00rater = 0.28, ICC = .22; female German targets: β = .21, SE = .04, t = 5.88, p < .001, σ2 = 3.93, τ00target = 0.73, τ00rater = 0.47, ICC = .23; male German targets: β = .11, SE = .03, t = 3.31, p < .001, σ2 = 3.22, τ00target = 0.43, τ00rater = 0.17, ICC = .16; non-significant interaction for male Brazilian targets: β = .07, SE = .04, t = 1.75, p = .08, σ2 = 2.21, τ00target = 0.41, τ00rater = 0.48, ICC = .29). For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = -.21, SE = .05, t = -4.03, p < .001, σ2 = 4.25, τ00target = 0.49, τ00rater = 0.27, ICC = .15, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.04, SE = .06, t = -0.71, p = .48, σ2 = 3.91, τ00target = 0.65, τ00rater = 0.61, ICC = .24, contrary to hypothesis 5). For German targets, there were no significant interactions terms, contrary to hypothesis 5 (Brazilian observers: β = .05, SE = .05, t = 1.13, p = .26, σ2 = 4.72, τ00target = 0.58, τ00rater = 0.25, ICC = .15; German observers: β = -.07, SE = .04, t = -1.57, p = .12, σ2 = 4.04, τ00target = 0.36, τ00rater = 0.48, ICC = .17). For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and both Brazilian observers (β = .12, SE = .05, t = 2.18, p = .003, σ2 = 5.95, τ00target = 0.91, τ00rater = 0.98, ICC = .24, more strongly positive association for male than for female targets, contrary to hypothesis 5) and German observers (β = -.13, SE = .05, t = -2.84, p = .004, σ2 = 5.19, τ00target = 0.53, τ00rater = 2.06, ICC = 0.33, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5). For German targets, the interactions were non-significant for both Brazilian observers (β = -.07, SE = .05, t = -1.38, p = .17, σ2 = 8.25, τ00target = 1.21, τ00rater = 0.37, ICC = .16) and German observers (β = -.04, SE = .04, t = -1.16, p = .25, σ2 = 5.96, τ00target = 0.26, τ00rater = 1.15, ICC = .19, both contrary to hypothesis 5). All interaction effects remained virtually unchanged when controlling for age, smiling, make-up, glasses, beardedness, and the headband worn by Brazilian targets.

Hypothesis 6 expected inter-observer agreements to be stronger intra-than interculturally (i.e. stronger for German observers judging German faces and Brazilian observers judging Brazilian faces compared to German observers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian observers judging German faces). This hypothesis was rejected for all of the attributes and target groups (no ICCs were larger for intra-than for intercultural judgments without overlap in confidence intervals, see Table 2; for one prosociality item (kindness) and for male as well as female German targets, the ICCs were larger without overlap in confidence intervals interthan intra-culturally, contrary to hypothesis 6). As predicted by hypothesis 7, we found mostly positive correlations between ratings by Brazilian and German observers across attributes and target groups (all rs > .24, ps < .001; except for familiarity for male German targets as hypothesised, r = .04, p = .66; the remaining three significant positive correlations for familiarity violated hypothesis 7; see Table 3).

Discussion

In this study, we provide a more focussed cross-population investigation of the attractiveness halo effect and gender differences therein, based on Brazilian and German facial stimuli. We replicated and extended earlier findings on the attractiveness halo effect (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000), showing mostly strong positive associations of perceived attractiveness with perceived intelligence, social competence, social dominance, prosociality, health, and familiarity (but not physical dominance) for male and female Brazilian and German targets and for Brazilian and German observers.

The attractiveness halo effect was found for all target groups, regardless of observer nationality (with a few exceptions for physical and social dominance, and intelligence for some target or observer groups, see Table 4). This confirms previous findings on the general crosscultural existence of the attractiveness halo effect (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Langlois et al., 2000). However, differences between observers from the two populations, one Western, more individualistic and the other non-Western, more collectivistic, did not manifest as hypothesised in this study, running counter to predictions by Wheeler and Kim (1997).

Interaction effects showed that associations were stronger for German observers in some cases, suggesting that people in Germany as a Western, more individualistic, and more developed country may generally be more susceptible to the attractiveness halo effect than those in Brazil as a non-Western, more collectivistic, and less developed country, although, as noted in the limitations, this interpretation cannot be disentangled from other differences between the two samples (e.g. socioeconomic status, urbanicity, recruitment context). The differences could still be due to attractiveness being more important for life outcomes in individualistic cultures, as people might experience greater agency in forming relationships and consequently in other relevant life outcomes (Anderson, 2019). Another possible explanation might be that in collectivistic countries individuals rely relatively more on the social reputation of someone than on self-inferred individual attributes. Crucially, our findings need to be replicated in further countries differing on cultural and socioecological dimensions, to ascertain the generalisability of our results.

Concerning the gender differences in familiarity and intelligence, hypothesis 5 predicting a stronger association for female than male targets was only partly confirmed (for intelligence for Brazilian targets and Brazilian observers only, but not for German targets or German observers; for familiarity for Brazilian targets judged by German observers only). For physical dominance, cross-population and target sex differences emerged. For male targets, perceived attractiveness was significantly positively correlated with physical dominance for cross-population ratings (i.e. Brazilian targets judged by German observers and German targets judged by Brazilian observers, non-significant for within-nationality ratings), only partly in line with hypothesis 2, the trade-off theory, and earlier studies within Western populations (DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004). Similarly, for perceived health, there were consistently stronger associations for German compared to Brazilian observers (for both target sexes, contrary to hypothesis 3). While the public healthcare system and the management and treatment of pathogen risks may still be better in Germany compared to Brazil, on average, and parasitic load is higher in Brazil (Celestino et al., 2021; Salmanton-García et al., 2025; Warnecke et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2025a , 2025b), we did not observe the hypothesised stronger positive correlation between target men's perceived attractiveness and physical dominance for Brazilian observers, but only a positive correlation for German observers. Similarly, our results do not confirm the prediction from trade-off theory that health preferences are stronger in countries with poorer public healthcare system or higher pathogen prevalence (DeBruine et al., 2010 (DeBruine et al., , 2012)). This may speak against the trade-off theory and the hypothesis that attractiveness is more strongly associated with masculinity (or physical dominance) and health preferences in cultures with higher pathogen prevalence or a poorer healthcare system (DeBruine et al., 2010 (DeBruine et al., , 2012;; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004; for conflicting evidence see Jones et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025). Alternatively, our measure of perceived physical dominance (with the item formulation focussing on strength and formidability) may be a weak measure of masculinity (though these concepts can be regarded as very close, e.g. Isen et al., 2015; Lukaszewski et al., 2016), or different indicators of masculinity across modalities not always intercorrelate reflecting different sensitivity to developmental phases of organisational masculinisation (Pereira, Varella et al., 2019; Varella et al., 2025). Our results may be a peculiarity of our observer samples. Presumably, most of the Brazilian observers who judged the target men's attractiveness and physical dominance were from the middle or upper social classes, recruited in university settings and most (68,5%) self-reported to be White (in contrast to 43,5% in the general population, Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística, 2022). Also, most Brazilian observers were from the cities of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, which are economically superior to most other regions in Brazil. This means that the generally higher pathogen prevalence and poorer healthcare system in Brazil may have been less relevant to the majority of our observer samples. These potential explanations should be investigated further in follow-up studies. Alternatively, in a re-analysis of the data from Debruine et al. (2010), Brooks et al. (2011) showed that rather than a national health index, women's preferences for masculinity were better explained by a country's income equality (see also Jones et al., 2021 and Lee et al., 2025 for further evidence conflicting with trade-off theory). This might explain why we did not find associations with judgments of physical dominance and health as predicted by trade-off theory, since our Brazilian observer samples were mainly composed of participants from the economically more developed cities of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. For female targets' physical dominance, there was no significant association for Brazilian targets and Brazilian observers (as hypothesised), but significant negative correlations for Brazilian and German targets among German observers (in line with Lee et al., 2017). Non-significant associations for Brazilian observers are in line with Zebrowitz et al. (1993) who studied observers from another collectivistic culture, Korea. Thus, observers from the non-Western, individualistic, and less developed country clearly differentiated by target sex when it comes to the attractiveness of more or less physically dominant faces, while for observers from the Western, more collectivistic, and more developed country there was no association at all (as suggested by Wheeler & Kim, 1997).

In contrast to physical dominance, attractiveness halo effects for social dominance were mostly positive (with varying effect sizes) for all target groups, with no difference by observer nationality (in line with Batres & Shiramizu, 2023), target nationality, or sex (with only a difference for Brazilian target womensignificant positive association for Brazilian observers and non-significant association for German observers, contrary to earlier findings, e.g. Maeng et al., 2022). These stronger positive halo effects emphasise that, compared to physical dominance, social dominance evokes weaker associations with threat potential and is typically more strongly linked to desirable traits (Anderson & Kilduff, 2009; Cheng et al., 2013). Hence, our findings stress the multi-facetted nature of dominance (e.g. Bryan et al., 2011).

For intelligence, there was only one significant moderation by target sex, namely for Brazilian observers judging Brazilian targets (positive association for male and negative for female targets), contrary to hypothesis 5 and earlier findings (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Kniffin et al., 2014). Generally, the positive and mostly significant correlations (all except for Brazilian males judged by Brazilians) between perceived intelligence and attractiveness are in line with earlier studies (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Zebrowitz et al., 2002), indicating that there are some facial cues from which intelligence is inferred which are also perceived as attractive.

The fact that attractiveness halo effects on intelligence perceptions were similar across both countries speaks against earlier suggestions that people in more individualistic countries like Germany may place a greater emphasis on competency-oriented attributes like intelligence (Shaffer et al., 2000; Wheeler & Kim, 1997).

The generally positive associations between perceived attractiveness and prosociality are in line with earlier studies (Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017). These positive associations were mostly stronger for German observers compared to Brazilian observers (except for male Brazilian targets), contradicting hypothesis 4 and earlier findings (e.g. Maeng et al., 2022; Wheeler & Kim, 1997; no difference in correlations for male targets). These larger associations for German compared to Brazilian observers, as the descriptively similar effects for social competence, run counter to earlier findings for communal attributes (e.g. Chen et al., 2016; Maeng et al., 2022; Wheeler & Kim, 1997). In our study, the more communal and affiliative attribute prosociality and social competence were not more strongly associated with perceived attractiveness for observers from a non-Western, more collectivistic, less developed compared to those from a Western, more individualistic, and more developed country. The smaller correlation for Brazilian observers could reflect cultural norms related to the stronger collectivism in Brazil, in that prosociality is considered a baseline trait, which is taken as given and people may not differ as much in their willingness to exhibit or expect prosocial behaviours as people in individualistic countries (see Levine et al., 2001 for experimental evidence of highest degrees of helping behaviour in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, compared to 22 cities in other countries). Hence, prosociality appears to be seen as more independent from appearance in Brazil (also evidenced by the non-significant correlation for female German targets and small positive correlation for female Brazilian targets, both for Brazilian observers).

The mostly stronger association of attractiveness with prosociality in Germany may be explicable by a more individualistic cultural orientation. A speculative post-hoc explanation may come from studies which showed that people from individualistic countries are more likely to rely on superficial cues such as physical appearance (e.g. facial features and linked attractiveness) in social judgments. For example, when judging personality traits (including social skills) from faces, Asian participants were slower in their judgments, whereas Western participants were more accurate and faster, regardless of the faces' cultural background (Walker et al., 2011). Moreover, people in individualistic cultures tend to frame relationships more strongly in terms of physical attractiveness, choosing friends and partners based on personal preferences and as a form of self-expression (Anderson et al., 2008). In contrast, people in more collectivistic cultures emphasise interdependence and embeddedness within family and community structures, with attractiveness playing a minor role. Our study is broadly consistent with, at least for evaluations of women, though this interpretation should be treated cautiously given the limitations of a two-country comparison.

The significant positive correlations of perceived familiarity with attractiveness for all four target groups could be seen as support for earlier claims that faces resembling oneself tend to be evaluated more positively than non-self-resembling faces (Todorov et al., 2015).

Alternatively, distinctiveness has been shown to cross-culturally affect perceived attractiveness negatively (Kleisner et al., 2024), and the opposite, facial averageness, positively (e.g. Jones & Jaeger, 2019; but see Fiala et al., 2021). Moderating effects by target sex were mixed, with a stronger positive association for female compared to male targets for German observers, in line with hypothesis 5 and with Kniffin and Wilson (2004), but stronger associations for male than female Brazilian targets judged by Brazilian observers, running counter to hypothesis 5.

Although our study supports previous findings of robust, positive attractiveness halo effects (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Langlois et al., 2000), effect sizes varied by attribute.

Attractiveness halo effects were strongest for perceived health, social competence, and (somewhat surprisingly) familiarity, and smaller for prosociality, intelligence, and especially for social and physical dominance, with some effects even going in the opposite direction for the latter two.

This pattern of results was similar, however, to those found in a meta-analysis including mostly Western studies by Eagly et al. (1991). Their meta-analysis showed largest effects for social competence, intermediate for potency and intellectual competence, and nearzero effects for concern for others, which are comparable to our attributes social/physical dominance, intelligence, and prosociality, respectively. Effect sizes in our study were largely comparable to those in the cross-cultural study by Batres and Shiramizu (2023), though overall smaller, particularly for physical dominance, which might be explained by the dominance item used.

Finally, interobserver agreements (ICCs) were not significantly larger for Brazilian observers judging Brazilian faces and German observers judging German faces compared to German observers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian observers judging German faces.

These results run counter to earlier results (e.g. Zebrowitz et al., 2012), the own-race effect (Tanaka et al., 2004), and our hypothesis 6. Such non-significant differences may be explicable by clearly stronger variation in cultural values within countries rather than between countries (Taras et al., 2016), especially in culturally, demographically, economically, and ecologically heterogeneous Brazil (Hofstede et al., 2010; Torres et al., 2015). However, our Brazilian observer sample was comparably homogenous, with 68,5% identifying as White, 21,4% as Brown, and only 10,1% as either Arabic, Black, Oriental, or Indigenous. Still, influences of cultural values should be explored further in halo effect research.

Implications

Our findings underline the meaningful implications of the attractiveness halo effect for social interaction, social life, and well-being. Langlois et al. (2000) conducted a meta-analysis showing that attractive children and adults are not only judged but also treated more positively than unattractive children and adults, even beyond zero-acquaintance interactions. These attractiveness biases spill over to numerous aspects of social and societal life. Attractive individuals, relative to more unattractive individuals, experience advantages in dating contexts (e.g. Eastwick et al., 2011), educational contexts (Abikoff et al., 1993; Dennis, 2007; Schmidt et al., 2023), on the labour market (Hosoda et al., 2003; Maestripieri et al., 2017), in politics (Olivola & Todorov, 2010; Palmer & Peterson, 2016), in health treatments (Martin et al., 1977; Napoleon et al., 1980), in court (Efran, 1974; Zebrowitz & McDonald, 1991), and regarding psychological well-being (Umberson & Hughes, 1987).

Attractive individuals are also preferred in social interactions and gatherings, and hence have better chances of developing more social capital than less attractive individuals (Palmer & Peterson, 2021). Nevertheless, not all social implications are positive, as higher facial femininity in women (as a proxy of attractiveness) may elicit stronger jealousy in mating rivals (Dong et al., 2025), and attractive individuals are thought of as less good parents compared to average-looking individuals (Cash & Duncan, 1984; Dion et al., 1972; bear in mind that these are rather dated findings which may have been based on now outdated stereotypes). On the other hand, less attractive individuals may face disadvantages due to their perceived unattractiveness, called negative halo effect, devils effect, or horns effect (Cook et al., 2003; Griffin & Langlois, 2006; Kordsmeyer et al., 2026; Radeke & Stahelski, 2020). Hence, while all attributes in this study were positively framed and connotated (except possibly physical dominance), future research should investigate negatively framed attributes and social consequences of low attractiveness in greater depth.

Despite the relatively strong attractiveness halo effects and their meaningful implications for person perception and social interactions, it is unclear whether face perceptions are valid predictors of individual characteristics and behaviour, or if the halo effect is primarily a cognitive bias resulting in invalid stereotypes. Investigations of actual associations of attractiveness with intelligence yielded mixed results (Breil et al., 2021; Driebe et al., 2021; Feingold, 1992; Mitchem et al., 2015; Kanazawa, 2011). In a study on intelligence and attractiveness in different age groups (from childhood to later adulthood, Zebrowitz et al., 2002), associations of perceived attractiveness were considerably stronger with perceived intelligence than with objectively measured intelligence (rs = .55-.64 versus rs .11-.26).

Similarly, findings on the relationship of perceived attractiveness with dominance, trustworthiness, and health measures or prosocial behaviour were mixed (Adolphs & Tusche, 2017; Arnocky & Davis, 2024; Bulczak & Gugushvili, 2023; Foo et al., 2017; Fruhen et al., 2015; Hansson et al., 2024; Hume & Montgomerie, 2001; Kordsmeyer et al., 2019; Skrinda et al., 2014; Thornhill & Gangestad, 2006; for a review see Weeden & Sabini, 2005). Such correlates of attractiveness with desirable outcomes and characteristics are likely not caused by attractiveness, but might emerge through self-fulfilling prophecies (e.g. Hill et al., 2023).

Limitations and future research

A methodological clarification is warranted. Classically, the attractiveness halo effect refers to an intra-observer bias in which one observer's judgment of attractiveness influences their evaluations of other attributes of the same target (Dion et al., 1972; Thorndike, 1920). Our design, using independent observer groups per attribute, yields between-group correlations and cannot isolate this pure intra-individual component from shared facial-cue covariation. This approach is nevertheless standard and is routinely labelled the "attractiveness halo effect".

Meta-analyses define the phenomenon as the consensual association between rated attractiveness and positive attributes, regardless of whether the same individuals supplied both ratings (Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000). Recent large-scale studies employing independent or randomly assigned observers per attribute interpret the resulting correlations identically (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Kordsmeyer et al., 2024; Kordsmeyer et al., 2026; Talamas et al., 2016).

One central limitation of the present study is that it only encompassed observers from two countries, one European and one South American. To increase the generalisability of our findings, our study should be replicated in further countries varying on cultural and socioecological dimensions like individualism-collectivism (cf. Minkov et al., 2017), including both targets and observers from these countries. Moreover, data in both countries were collected predominantly in university settings. University-educated participants, especially those from major urban centres such as São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, may share more similar values, norms, and cognitive styles than the broader national populations, potentially attenuating the cultural distance the study aimed to examine. Besides the attributes investigated in this study, further attributes crucially relevant to social interactions and hence to person perception should be investigated regarding possible cross-cultural nuances in attractiveness halo effects, such as warmth, emotional stability, confidence, or happiness (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Fiske et al., 2007). These and similar attributes have been examined for potential halo effects, albeit seldom with a full cross-cultural perspective for stimuli and observers (cf. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023).

A further limitation concerns the use of facial photos to assess perceptions of socially relevant attributes. Although a recent meta-analysis demonstrated ecological validity of photobased attractiveness judgments (Kaschel & Hildebrandt, 2023) and the face is a central source of social information (Currie & Little, 2009), these static facial stimuli capture only a proportion of socially relevant cues. Hence, future studies should include additional modalities, such as vocal and olfactory stimuli (Demattè et al., 2007; Kordsmeyer et al., 2020; Pereira, Varella et al., 2019; Saxton et al., 2009; Trebicky et al., 2023), as well as bodily stimuli (Kordsmeyer et al., 2024; Pereira, Silva et al., 2019). Furthermore, contemporarily popular beautification or appearance enhancement strategies reportedly augment perceived attractiveness, such as in social media or using makeup or plastic surgery, but distort typical associations with other socially relevant attributes. For example, Liang et al. (2023) showed that women's faces after plastic surgery were perceived as more trustworthy and more attractive than natural faces or faces wearing makeup. However, when observers were informed about the plastic surgery, trustworthiness judgments declined considerably. In another study, minimally invasive facial aesthetic treatment led to a small, but significant increase in perceived attractiveness (especially as a short-term, but not as a long-term partner), but not in trustworthiness (Jaeger et al., 2025). Further, attractiveness halo effects on perceived intelligence and trustworthiness were still detected after applying an AI-based beauty filter to facial photos rendering the faces more attractive. However, they were weaker compared to effects for the original faces (Gulati et al., 2024). In our study, we had no knowledge of any plastic surgery, but coded female targets' makeup and male targets' beardedness. Controlling for these factors, associations of attractiveness with the other attributes remained mostly unchanged. Bivariate associations between Brazilian and German target men's beardedness and attractiveness were close to zero and non-significant (in line with Dixon & Vasey, 2012; in contrast to Dixson & Brooks, 2013; Dixson et al., 2016). For makeup, a small but significant positive correlation was found for German target women (as in Mileva et al., 2016; Schneider & Moron, 2023) and somewhat surprisingly a small negative, significant correlation for Brazilian target women. Splitting the latter by observer nationality showed that only for German observers (i.e. cross-population ratings) the association was significantly negative (small nonsignificant negative association for Brazilian observers). Possible interpretations for the latter include a stronger naturalness preference for German men judging Brazilian women or cultural differences in evaluation of the targets' makeup (Cunningham et al., 1995; Etcoff et al., 2011).

However, it needs to be kept in mind that the association between makeup and attractiveness was positive for German target women. Because makeup was not experimentally manipulated, the association may also reflect unmeasured characteristics correlated with makeup, such as self-presentation style, or other facial and contextual cues (Penton-Voak et al., 2004).

So far, most research on halo effects has focused exclusively on associations on the side of targets and stimuli. In this study, we analysed individual ratings in cross-classified multilevel models that included random intercepts for targets and observers (and, where relevant, observer nationality). Although the multilevel models account for individual differences in overall scale use via observer random intercepts, cultural differences in response style (e.g. extreme versus central tendency) between Brazilian and German observers could still affect mean-level comparisons (Table 3) and, potentially, correlational patterns. Future work could more explicitly model extreme response style to further rule out this alternative explanation. Further, while these models account for overall observer-level variance, they do not examine specific inter-individual differences in cognitive and personality-related characteristics, which likely strongly influence person perception, including halo effects. First, in our study we employed groups of either other-sex or same-sex observers, depending on the attribute. Specifically, only for attractiveness and intelligence (attributes prominent in mate choice) observer sex converged, whereas for the other attributes observer sex (same-sex judgments due to their relevance in intrasexual competition) differed from attractiveness. This divergence may complicate the comparability of the strength of halo effects, given that earlier studies showed that observer sex affects judgments of attractiveness (Marcus & Miller, 2003). While a metaanalysis found no consistent observer-sex differences in halo effects (Eagly et al., 1991), observer sex may still matter. In particular, a sexual attribution bias has been proposed whereby highly attractive individuals receive more critical judgments from same-sex (but not other-sex) observers, for example in simulated job interviews (Agthe et al., 2011; Försterling et al., 2007; see also Agthe et al., 2023 on intrasexual competition and the derogation of attractive rivals).

Because our design obtained attractiveness ratings only from other-sex observers and the maximum attractiveness ratings (averages per target) across all four target groups remained well below the scale's positive endpoint (see Table 3), we could not test for such a non-linear penalty or sexual attribution bias (for recent exploratory evidence contrary to this bias, see Kordsmeyer et al., 2026). Further, observers' conceptual trait associations (e.g. believing trustworthy people are also kind; Illithova et al., 2025), self-construals (Markus & Kitayama, 1991), own dominance (Watkins et al., 2010 (Watkins et al., , 2012)), current mood (Forgas, 2011; Laham & Forgas, 2022), or own attractiveness and intelligence (Sim et al., 2015) could be investigated as moderators of cross-cultural differences.

For deeper insights into the mechanisms of halo effects, future research should examine facial cues as predictors or moderators of correlations between perceptions of socially relevant attributes. For example, cross-cultural differences in associations of perceived facial attractiveness with facial morphological sexual dimorphism and averageness were shown across five distant countries (in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Latin America, Fiala et al., 2021). On the other hand, attractiveness perceptions were consistently negatively affected by facial distinctiveness across ten countries worldwide (Kleisner et al., 2024). Earlier claims of positive effects of facial symmetry on attractiveness perceptions were refuted in more recent studies (e.g. Jones & Jaeger, 2019; Kleisner et al., 2024). Similarly, associations of facial masculinity or facial femininity on men's or women's attractiveness, respectively, appear not to be robust or large (e.g. Jones & Jaeger, 2019; Kleisner et al., 2024). Some of these more objective measures have been shown to relate to perceptions of physical dominance, prosociality, and health instead (Foo et al., 2017; Kleisner et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2023). Finally, for a better understanding of cross-cultural variations in halo effects, contextual factors such as locally perceived violence, pathogen prevalence, mate preferences, and climate should be included in future studies (e.g. Bromham et al., 2018; Borras-Guevara et al., 2017; DeBruine et al., 2010). These measures should be investigated further for a more complete understanding of cross-cultural nuances in halo effects and mechanisms of person perception generally.

Conclusion

This study extends earlier findings on cross-population nuances of the attractiveness halo effect based on faces as a persistent cognitive bias in person perception. Overall, associations with the perceived attractiveness of several socially relevant attributes were similar for observers from a non-Western, more collectivistic, less developed country (Brazil) as for observers from a Western, more individualistic, more developed country (Germany), and for both male and female targets. Consistently positive correlations were found for health, social competence, and unexpectedly familiarity, and mostly positive correlations for social dominance, prosociality, and intelligence. In contrast, associations were mixed for physical dominance by target gender and nationality. In conclusion, this study demonstrates very similar perceptions across the two populations for a range of socially relevant attributes. Thus, only limited cross-population differences in halo effects in our study mostly run counter to hypotheses based on earlier theoretical and empirical suggestions. These findings add to our understanding of biases in person perception and why more positive social outcomes are often experienced by more attractive people.

Open Science Statement.

The data, analysis script, and materials are available at https://osf.io/puxf2/overview?view_only=69fca548052c4684ad29441c0a2113a2 and the preregistration at https://osf.io/xr8v7/overview?view_only=4ada5023d7194afd833a999dd28424ed.

Appendix Preregistered analyses based on aggregate ratings for hypotheses 1-5

For each observer group (separately for target sex, target nationality, observer nationality, and attribute), ratings were aggregated and mean values were used in further analyses. As preregistered, preliminary analyses used t-tests to assess mean differences in ratings between Brazilian and German observers for each attribute and target group. Pearson correlations were calculated to examine bivariate associations of perceived attractiveness with perceived physical dominance, social dominance, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity. Linear regression models were run for moderator effects of observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) (with perceived attractiveness and either observer nationality or target sex as the predictor variables plus their interaction term, and a second attribute as the outcome variable). As preregistered, one-sided tests were used for directional hypotheses (Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016). To investigate the robustness of our findings, we ran partial correlations and linear regression models including the preregistered control variables target age (e.g. see Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014), target relationship status (binary: single vs. open relationship/committed relationship/engaged/married), and target BMI.

As further control variables, we added targets' smiling, target men's beardedness, as well as target women's make-up and jewellery. Furthermore, the strength of associations between Brazilian and German observers on the same attributes were compared employing moderation analyses in regression models.

Bivariate Pearson correlations of attractiveness with all other attributes are shown in Table S1, stratified by target group and observer nationality. For all target groups and both observer nationalities, perceived attractiveness correlated positively with perceived health, social competence, and familiarity (confirming hypothesis 1). Perceived attractiveness correlated positively with perceived intelligence for all target groups except for male Brazilian targets rated by Brazilian observers (for which we found a non-significant, yet positive association), with perceived prosociality for all target groups except for female German targets judged by Brazilian observers, and with perceived social dominance for all target groups except for female Brazilian targets judged by German observers (mostly in line with hypothesis 1). Finally, for perceived physical dominance, there were significant positive correlations with perceived attractiveness for male targets (for both target nationalities, only for male German but not Brazilian observers, contrary to hypothesis 2), and significant negative correlations for female targets (again for both target nationalities, though only for male German but not Brazilian observers, see Table S1, partially confirming hypothesis 2).

Almost all correlations remained virtually unchanged when controlling for age, smiling, make-up, glasses, beardedness, and the headband worn by Brazilian targets (see Table S2).

To test hypotheses 3 to 5 on cross-cultural and sex differences, linear regression models were run including interaction terms between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) predicting a second attribute. For all four target group, the association between perceived attractiveness and health was significantly stronger for German compared to Brazilian observers (contrary to hypothesis 3, interaction term for male Brazilian targets: β = .25, SE = .07, t = 3.43, p < .001; interaction term for female Brazilian targets: β = .22, SE = .08, t = 2.95, p = .003; interaction term for male German targets: β = .30, SE = .09, t = 3.19, p = .002; interaction term for female German targets: β = .25, SE = .08, t = 2.90, p = .004). For male German but not Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction term between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality on prosociality, with a significantly stronger association for German observers, contrary to hypothesis 4 (for male German targets: β = .15, SE = .07, t = 2.22, p = .03; male Brazilian targets: β = .14, SE = .07, t = 1.92, p = .056). For female targets, there were significant interactions on prosociality for Brazilian targets (β = .37, SE = .09, t = 4.05, p < .001) and German targets (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005), with a positive association for German observers and a negative association for Brazilian observers, contrary to our hypothesis 4. For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.06, SE = .09, t = -0.71, p = .48). For German targets, there were no significant interactions terms, contrary to hypothesis 5 (Brazilian observers: β = -.004, SE = .08, t = -0.05, p = .96; German observers: β = -.12, SE = .08, t = -1.55, p = .12). For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and both Brazilian observers (β = .29, SE = .09, t = 3.41, p < .001, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, contrary to hypothesis 5) and German observers (β = -.25, SE = .09, t = -2.87, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5). For German targets, there was a significant interaction for Brazilian observers (β = -.31, SE = .11, t = -2.81, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.09, SE = .08, t = -1.16, p = .25, contrary to hypothesis 5).

Regression models with attractiveness as the dependent variable (hypotheses 3-5)

For robustness checks, as preregistered, linear regression models were run with perceived attractiveness as the dependent variable and observer nationality and a second attribute as the two independent variables plus their interaction terms. First, there was no significant interaction for perceived health for male or female Brazilian targets (male targets: β = .13, SE = .14, t = 0.92, p = .36; female targets: β = -.03, SE = .08, t = -0.35, p = .73; both different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 3), but only for male German targets (β = .25, SE = .10, t = 2.44, p = .02, stronger positive for German observers than for Brazilian observers, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 3; non-significant for female German targets: β = .05, SE = .11, t = 0.40, p = .69, different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 3). Second, for prosociality, there was only one significant interaction (for female Brazilian targets: β = .48, SE = .19, t = 2.52, p = .01, positive association for German observers and negative association for Brazilian observers, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4; male Brazilian targets: β = -.06, SE = .22, t = -0.25, p = .80, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4; male German targets: β = .04, SE = .16, t = 0.26, p = .80; female German targets: β = .27, SE = .14, t = 1.90, p = .058, for the latter two different from significant interactions with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4).

For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = -.96, SE = .19, t = -5.09, p < .001, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from significant interaction in opposite direction with attractiveness as independent variable and now contrary to hypothesis 5) and for German observers (β = -.41, SE = .12, t = -3.44, p < .001, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, still contrary to hypothesis 5). For German targets, there was a significant interaction for German observers (β = -.24, SE = .11, t = -2.31, p = .02, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, still contrary to hypothesis 5), but not Brazilian observers (β = -.19, SE = .15, t = -1.27, p = .22, similar to non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 5). For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and German observers (β = -.37, SE = .11, t = -3.32, p = .001, stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, similar to significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still in line with hypothesis 5; non-significant for Brazilian observers: β = .20, SE = .16, t = 1.30, p = .20, different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 5) as well as for German targets (Brazilian observers: β = -.25, SE = .10, t = -2.41, p = .02, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, but now in line with hypothesis 5; German observers: β = .44, SE = .09, t = 4.79, p < .001, stronger positive for male targets, different from nonsignificant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 5).

Results

We had initially preregistered perceived attractiveness as the outcome variable, however, analysing it as the predictor variable is more in line with how the attractiveness halo effect is understood theoretically and empirically, e.g.Langlois et al.,

Results of preregistered analyses with attractiveness as outcome variable can be found in the supplement, with the statistical significance and direction of interaction effects being mostly identical to the updated results reported in the main text, with only one deviation for one target/observer nationality combination for familiarity (hypothesis 5).
